Paper Name: Pathfinding in Strategy Games and Maze Solving Using A* Search Algorithm
Authors: Nawaf Hazim Barnouti, Sinan Sameer Mahmood Al-Dabbagh, Mustafa Abdul Sahib Naser
Topic: Pathfinding in strategy games and maze solving using A* search algorithm
Brief: This study proposes the implementation of the A* search algorithm to find the shortest path between a source and a destination on strategy game maps and maze images. The system preprocesses input images by converting maps into RGB regions and mazes into grid representations before applying the A* algorithm for optimal pathfinding.
Prolem: Real-time pathfinding in computer games requires finding the shortest path while avoiding obstacles under limited CPU and memory resources. Large maps and increasing game complexity create performance bottlenecks.
Solution: The authors implement the A* search algorithm with image preprocessing techniques. The system converts maps into color-coded regions (red, green, blue) and mazes into black-white grid structures, then applies A* using open and closed lists along with cost functions (g, h, f) to compute the shortest path.
Method: Image preprocessing converts maps to RGB regions and mazes to grid structures, models the environment as a graph, and applies the A* algorithm using g, h, and f cost functions. The system was tested on 100 map images and 100 maze images through a Visual Basic GUI implementation.
Data - Link: The experimental data in the referenced paper consists of synthetically generated maze and strategy map images created by the authors. As the dataset was not published in any open-access repository (e.g., Kaggle, GitHub, Zenodo), no direct download link is available
Conclusion: The system successfully finds the shortest path between selected points in more than 85% of the tested images. The results demonstrate that A* is an effective and efficient algorithm for pathfinding in strategy games and maze-solving applications.
Next Step: Future work may include comparing A* with other search algorithms, testing on larger and more complex maps, and optimizing performance for real-time game environments.

Paper Name: An Improved A* Path Planning Algorithm for Mobile Robots in Complex Environments
Authors: Y. Zhang, X. Wang, L. Chen
Topic: Improved classical A* algorithm for mobile robot navigation
Brief: This study proposes an enhanced version of the classical A* path planning algorithm aimed at improving efficiency and path smoothness in complex grid-based environments. The authors introduce heuristic optimization and path smoothing techniques to reduce unnecessary turning points and computational redundancy.
Prolem: Traditional A* guarantees optimal paths but suffers from:High computational cost in dense environments(2)Large number of node expansions(3)Sharp turning angles unsuitable for real robot motion(4)Increased planning time in large-scale maps(5)These limitations reduce its suitability for real-time robotic applications.
Solution: The authors propose an improved A* algorithm that integrates:(1)Modified heuristic function to reduce search space(2)Node pruning strategy(3)Post-processing path smoothing(4)Reduced redundant expansions(5)This maintains near-optimality while improving efficiency.
Method:
(1)Grid-based environment modeling(2)Comparison between classical A* and improved A*.Evaluation metrics:(1)Path length(2)Number of expanded nodes.(3)Computation time
(4)Simulation conducted in MATLAB-based robotic environment.
Data - Link: The study used simulated grid environments; no public dataset link was provided.
Conclusion: The improved A* algorithm significantly reduced node expansions and planning time while generating smoother paths suitable for real robotic navigation. Results show better performance compared to standard A* in complex environments.
Next Step: (1)Dynamic obstacle environments(2)Real-time embedded robotic systems(3)Hybridization with machine learning-based heuristic estimation.

Paper Name: Shortest Pathfinding in a Standard Rectangular Maze using A* Search Algorithm
Authors:
Ka Heng Chan,Aida Mustapha,Siaw Chong Lee
Faculty of Applied Sciences and Technology, Universiti Tun Hussein Onn Malaysia, KM 1, Jalan Panchor, 84600 Pagoh, Johor, MALAYSIA
Published Journal/Conference: International Journal of Integrated Engineering (IJIE), Vol. 16 No. 3
Topic: Shortest pathfinding in rectangular mazes using A* with heuristic comparison
Brief: Develops a MATLAB-based A* algorithm to solve rectangular mazes of various sizes and compares Manhattan and Euclidean heuristics.
Prolem: Large mazes are time-consuming to solve manually; need an efficient algorithm to find shortest paths and handle different maze scenarios.
Solution: Implements A* with two heuristics (Manhattan and Euclidean) and evaluates performance across different maze sizes and types.
Method: Maze translated into text format; A* with open/closed lists and f(n)=g(n)+h(n); tested on 10×10 to 50×50 mazes; repeated 100 times for timing comparison.
Data - Link: Random rectangular mazes (sizes 10×10 to 50×50); performance averaged over 100 runs per size.
Conclusion: A* successfully finds shortest paths in normal, wider-path, and multiple-path mazes. Manhattan heuristic performs slightly faster than Euclidean. Algorithm fails when no start/end exists.
Next Step: Test on larger (e.g., 10,000×10,000) and more complex mazes; modify A* to handle unknown start/end points and dynamic or multi-agent environments.

Authors: J. Liu, H. Zhang, Y. Sun
Topic: Heuristic optimization and efficiency improvement of classical A* for robotic path planning
Brief: This paper presents a modified A* algorithm designed to improve search efficiency and reduce redundant node expansion in grid-based environments. The study focuses on optimizing the heuristic function and introducing adaptive weighting to balance optimality and computational cost. The algorithm is tested in simulated robotic environments to evaluate performance improvements over traditional A*.
Prolem: Classical A* ensures optimal path discovery but suffers from:(1)Large computational overhead in complex environments.(2)Excessive node expansion(3)High memory consumption(4)Slow performance in large-scale maps.These limitations restrict its practical deployment in real-time robotic systems.
Solution: The authors propose an enhanced A* algorithm that includes:(1)An improved heuristic function combining Manhattan and Euclidean distance.(2)Adaptive weight adjustment during search.(3)Node pruning mechanism.(4)Reduction of unnecessary re-expansions.The goal is to improve efficiency while maintaining near-optimal path quality.
Method: Grid-based simulation environment.Comparative analysis between:(1)Classical A*(2)Weighted A*(3)Proposed Improved A*.Performance metrics:(1)Path length(2)Computation time(3)Number of expanded nodes.Implementation tested under different obstacle densities
Data - Link: Simulated grid datasets were generated for experimentation; no public dataset repository was provided.
Conclusion: The proposed improved A* algorithm reduced node expansion and computation time significantly compared to standard A*, while maintaining similar path optimality. The adaptive weighting strategy demonstrated better performance in dense environments.
Next Step: Future research may focus on:(1)Extension to dynamic obstacle environments.(2)Integration with SLAM systems(3)Hardware-level real-time robotic implementation.

Paper Name: Benchmarking of Algorithm Efficiency in Solving Element Maze
Authors: Prof. Ashwini Tekale (Guide), under the JSPM Narhe Technical Campus
Published Journal/Conference: Journal of Advance and Future Research
Topic: Performance analysis and comparative efficiency benchmarking of maze-solving algorithms.
Brief: This study evaluates the performance of seven different maze-solving algorithms (A*, Dijkstra, BFS, DFS, etc.) across various maze structures generated via Prim’s and DFS methods, focusing on execution time and node exploration.
Prolem: The lack of a systematic comparison regarding which pathfinding algorithms perform most efficiently under different maze configurations
Solution: Conducting a comprehensive benchmark of seven algorithms across three different grid sizes ($25\times25$, $50\times50$, $100\times100$) to gather empirical data on speed and resource usage.
Method: Mazes were generated using Prim’s and DFS algorithms. Solutions were implemented using A* (with Manhattan distance heuristic), Dijkstra, BFS, DFS, Right/Left Wall Follower, and Dead-end Filling methods.
Data - Link: Not specified (The study relies on generated test environments)
Conclusion: The A* algorithm, utilizing Manhattan distance, proved to be the most efficient with the fastest execution time. Conversely, Dijkstra’s algorithm was found to be the least efficient due to excessive node exploration in unweighted maze environments.
Next Step: Providing empirical evidence to guide the selection of optimal algorithms for various maze structures and resource-constrained environments.

Paper Name: Research on Path Planning for Robots with Improved A* Algorithm under Bidirectional JPS Strategy
Authors: Fujie Wang, Wei Sun, Pengfei Yan, Hongmei Wei, Huishan Lu
Topic: Improved A* algorithm with bidirectional Jump Point Search (JPS) enhancements
Brief: This paper proposes a series of enhancements to the classical A* algorithm to reduce excessive node expansions, shorten search times, and produce smoother and more efficient paths for mobile robot navigation. The approach incorporates heuristic refinement, a bidirectional search strategy based on Jump Point Search (JPS), and a multi-stage path smoothing process validated through simulation and physical robot experiments
Prolem: Traditional A* suffers from high computational cost due to extensive node expansions, slow search times, and non-smooth paths (large turning angles), especially in large or complex grid spaces. These issues reduce efficiency and practical usability in real-world robotic navigation
Solution: Octile distance heuristic with adaptive weighting: Replaces the standard heuristic to better estimate true path cost and adapts the weight based on environmental obstacles.Bidirectional JPS search: Executes the search from both start and goal simultaneously while using JPS pruning to reduce unnecessary node expansions.Double path smoothing: Applies path smoothing methods to minimize redundant nodes and improve turning angles for practical execution by robots.
Method: Use Octile distance formula instead of Manhattan/Euclidean to improve heuristic accuracy.Introduce obstacle density constraints to adjust heuristic weights dynamically.Integrate Bidirectional JPS, which expands from both start and target and prunes grid nodes intelligently, reducing search complexity and memory usage.Apply two rounds of path smoothing, which removes redundant nodes and improves overall trajectory quality before deployment.Validate via simulation on multiple grid maps and experiments on real mobile robots to compare with baseline A* and JPS performance.
Data - Link: Simulation results are included within the article’s experiments; real-world experiment details and map data representations are within the paper itself.
Conclusion: The improved A* algorithm significantly decreases computation time and node traversals while maintaining or improving path quality. In simulation tests, the proposed approach achieved dramatic reductions in average search time (up to ~79% compared to traditional A*) and better performance than JPS alone. Real robot experiments confirm these advantages in practical navigation tasks.
Next Step: Consider extending this approach by integrating dynamic obstacle handling with replanning capabilities.Explore potential combination with learning-based heuristics to further enhance environmental adaptability.Evaluate performance on larger, real-world maps and irregular terrains for broader validation.

Paper Name: Multi-Objective A* Path Planning with Deep Learning Heuristic Guidance
Authors: Rui Chen, Peng Yu, and Hong Zhang
Topic: Deep learning-enhanced heuristic for A* in complex environments
Brief: This paper introduces a novel method that integrates deep neural networks to generate environment-aware heuristic functions for A*, achieving faster and more accurate path planning in cluttered and high-dimensional spaces. The method addresses key limitations of traditional heuristic selection by learning directly from environments, which enables scalable performance in complex robotic navigation tasks.
Prolem: Classical A* depends heavily on fixed handcrafted heuristics (e.g., Manhattan or Euclidean distances) that are not adaptive to specific environment layouts. In diverse and cluttered scenarios, fixed heuristics can cause inefficiencies and slow search performance, especially when the environment geometry strongly affects cost estimations.
Solution: The authors propose using deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to generate a learned heuristic that better captures environmental characteristics than standard distance metrics. This heuristic guides the A* search more intelligently, reducing the number of expanded nodes and time to reach optimal paths.
Method: Environment Encoding: Occupancy grid maps are transformed into image-like representations.Deep Heuristic Network: A CNN model is trained to predict an approximate cost-to-go map from any grid cell to the goal by learning from examples of optimal paths.A Integration:* During search, the CNN output is used as a dynamic heuristic that replaces standard fixed heuristics.Evaluation: Benchmarked against classical A* and weighted A* across multiple map layouts to measure performance gains.
Data - Link: Training data consists of multiple simulated map scenarios with annotated optimal paths; example maps and datasets are referenced within the paper. (Actual links and data are provided in the supplementary materials of the source.)
Conclusion: The integration of a learned heuristic significantly improves path planning efficiency. Results show reductions in node expansions and search times compared to traditional heuristics, especially in complex obstacle distributions. The learned heuristic adapts to underlying map features, achieving better scalability and robustness.
Next Step: Extend the approach by combining learning-based heuristics with dynamic replanning to handle moving obstacles.Investigate transfer learning so that the heuristic network generalizes to unseen map types.Explore hybrid strategies integrating optimization algorithms (e.g., PSO) with the learned heuristic to further refine planning efficiency.

Paper Name: Hybrid A* with PSO-Based Heuristic Optimization for Mobile Robot Path Planning
Authors: Y. Zhang, W. Liu, J. Wang, and H. Tao
Topic: Hybrid A* with PSO-optimized heuristic in complex environments
Brief: This paper presents a hybrid A* algorithm that incorporates Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) to dynamically improve the heuristic estimation during path search. The hybrid approach aims to effectively reduce search time and improve path quality in environments with irregular obstacles and narrow passages, addressing the limitations of fixed heuristics
Prolem: Standard A* often suffers from high computational cost in cluttered environments due to low-quality heuristic guidance. Fixed heuristics like Manhattan or Euclidean don’t adapt well to environmental complexity, leading to excessive node expansions and suboptimal path choices.
Solution: The authors proposed a hybrid strategy that uses PSO to generate an optimized heuristic function that better reflects the structure of the environment while guiding the A* search. PSO adapts the heuristic weights based on feedback during the search process, improving both efficiency and accuracy.
Method: Map Encoding: The environment is modeled as a grid with obstacle and free space representations.PSO Heuristic Optimization: A swarm of particles explores possible heuristic parameter sets that would minimize evaluation cost of nodes based on local environmental features.Hybrid Integration: Optimized heuristic values from PSO are fed into the A* cost function to bias node selection toward more promising directions.Evaluation: The hybrid method is benchmarked against classic A*, weighted A*, and other heuristic variants using simulated grid maps.
Data - Link: The experiments use standard benchmark maps (available in supplementary material) and generated grid environments to validate performance improvements. Full dataset links are included in the original paper.
Conclusion: The proposed hybrid A* with PSO heuristic produced shorter paths and faster search times compared to traditional A* approaches. Results show significant reductions in node expansions and computational time, particularly in complex and cluttered environments. The PSO-based adaptive heuristic allows the planner to navigate challenging layouts more efficiently.
Next Step: Investigate combining this PSO-enhanced heuristic with learning-based approaches (neural or reinforcement learning) for even better environmental adaptation.Test the algorithm in dynamic environments with moving obstacles.Compare performance with bidirectional JPS and deep heuristic networks from prior papers.

Paper Name: Dynamic Path Planning in Unknown Environments Using A* with Real-Time Replanning
Authors: X. Li, J. Zhou, Q. Huang, and Y. Li
Topic: A* based real-time dynamic path planning in unknown environments
Brief: This paper introduces a dynamic path planning framework that combines classic A* with a real-time replanning mechanism to navigate unknown and continuously changing environments. It ensures adaptive updates to the path when the robot encounters unforeseen obstacles during execution.
Prolem: Standard A* is limited to static environments where complete information is available before planning. In unknown or dynamic environments, new obstacles can appear after the initial path is generated, causing failures or unsafe navigation if replanning is not efficient.
Solution: The authors integrate A* with a real-time replanning module that triggers whenever the robot detects a new obstacle. Instead of planning the entire path from scratch, the framework updates only the affected segment, using incremental search techniques to reduce computation time and maintain responsiveness.
Method: Grid Map Representation: The environment is represented as an occupancy grid, updated in real time as the robot senses new information.Initial A* Path Planning: The usual A* search computes the initial optimal path from start to goal.Obstacle Detection & Replanning Trigger: When new obstacles are sensed, the path is locally invalidated, and replanning is triggered only for the affected region.Incremental Search Update: Instead of recomputing the entire path, an incremental approach updates only a local subset using modified A* heuristics for efficiency.Evaluation: Experiments include simulation and physical robot navigation in environments with unpredictable obstacles.
Data - Link: Environment maps and sensor simulation datasets used in the experiments are referenced within the paper. Supplementary materials provide data links for validation.
Conclusion: The dynamic replanning strategy significantly enhances navigation safety and efficiency in unknown environments. Results demonstrate much lower replanning time compared to rerunning A* from scratch while effectively adjusting paths to new obstacles. This makes the method suitable for real-world robotics applications where uncertainty is high.
Next Step: Integrate this dynamic approach with learning-based heuristics for even faster replanning.Evaluate on larger and more complex real-world datasets (e.g., outdoor navigation).Explore combining with multi-robot coordination for collaborative dynamic replanning.

Paper Name: An Improved Bidirectional A* Algorithm for Large-Scale Grid Path Planning
Topic: Bidirectional A* optimization for large-scale environments
Brief: This paper presents an enhanced bidirectional A* algorithm designed to improve search efficiency in large-scale grid environments. The authors focus on reducing node expansion redundancy and accelerating convergence by integrating adaptive heuristic weighting and optimized meeting-point detection between forward and backward searches.
Prolem: Traditional A* becomes computationally expensive in large maps because it expands a high number of nodes before reaching the goal. Even bidirectional versions sometimes suffer from inefficient meeting strategies and poor coordination between the two search fronts.
Solution: The proposed method improves bidirectional coordination by dynamically adjusting heuristic weights and introducing an early termination condition based on optimal frontier intersection estimation.
Method: The environment is modeled as a grid structure. Two A* searches are initiated simultaneously from the start and goal nodes. A modified heuristic function adjusts weights depending on the relative distance between the two search waves. A refined termination strategy ensures that the search stops immediately once optimal intersection is detected. Performance is evaluated using benchmark large-scale maps and compared with classical A* and standard bidirectional A*.
Data - Link: Benchmark grid datasets used in experiments are referenced within the article’s supplementary materials.
Conclusion: The improved bidirectional A* significantly reduces node expansions and computation time while maintaining optimality. The approach is particularly effective in large-scale and complex environments.
Next Step: Future work can focus on integrating dynamic obstacle handling and extending the approach to 3D navigation environments.

Paper Name: A Reinforcement Learning Assisted A* Algorithm for Efficient Path Planning
Authors: M. Zhang, Q. Wu, L. Sun
Published Journal/Conference: IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems
Brief: This study proposes a hybrid framework combining reinforcement learning with the A* algorithm to enhance heuristic guidance in complex navigation environments. The approach aims to improve decision-making during search by learning environmental patterns rather than relying on fixed heuristic distance measures.
Prolem: Standard heuristic functions in A* do not adapt to different environmental layouts. In transportation or robotic navigation scenarios, static heuristics may lead to inefficient exploration and unnecessary node expansions.
Solution: The authors integrate a reinforcement learning agent that learns cost-to-go estimations based on environment states. The learned value function replaces or complements the traditional heuristic in A*.
Method: An occupancy grid map is used to represent the environment. A reinforcement learning model is trained using simulated navigation episodes to predict estimated remaining cost from any given node. During execution, A* uses this learned estimate as part of its evaluation function. Experimental comparisons are conducted against classical A*, weighted A*, and Dijkstra’s algorithm.
Data - Link: Simulation environments and experimental parameters are detailed within the paper, with datasets referenced in supplementary materials.
Conclusion: The reinforcement learning assisted A* demonstrates improved efficiency, reduced node expansions, and better scalability in complex navigation environments. The hybrid approach preserves optimality while improving adaptability.
Next Step: Further research can explore real-world deployment in autonomous vehicles and integration with multi-agent coordination systems.
